text:
Lynn Conway was an early pioneer in the field of VLSI (Very-Large-Scale Integration) design. Initially, she was a shy individual in New York, who experienced gender dysphoria and attempted a gender transition. After withdrawing from MIT in 1959, she continued her education at Columbia University's School of Engineering and Applied Science, earning her B.S. and M.S.E.E. degrees in 1962 and 1963.
She worked at IBM Research on the Advanced Computing Systems (ACS) project, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling, an architecture later noted by the Computer History Museum as the first 'superscalar' design. After completing her gender transition in 1968, Conway restarted her career as a contract programmer and later as a digital system designer at Memorex. At Xerox PARC starting in 1973, she co-founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology and, collaborating with Ivan Sutherland and Carver Mead, co-authored *Introduction to VLSI Systems* , which became a standard textbook. She further contributed to simplifying chip design through the invention of dimensionless, scalable design rules and institutionalizing the Metal Oxide Semiconductor Implementation Service (MOSIS) system in 1981.
